lines.text: Your grandpa died 9 days ago.
But at 3 a.m., he picks up the phone. And you have 60 seconds before you lose him forever.
Kiddo? Is that you?
Grandpa?!
Listen. I don't have long. Don't let them sell the house. The blue tin. Second drawer. Tell your grandma I...
Click. The line goes dead. Exactly 60 seconds.
Over the next 30 days, you'll talk to Albert Einstein, make 86,000 dollars, and find out how that sentence ends.
Here's how it works. It's Grandpa's old rotary phone. Dial anyone who has ever died, and they pick up.
You get exactly 60 seconds. One call a day. And every person only once.
Grandpa already used his.
More than 100 billion people have ever lived. You get to choose 30.
The next morning, you go to Grandma's.
The bank wants 86,000 dollars by the end of the month. Or the house goes.
The house. With the blue tin inside.
It's only a house, sweetheart. Fifty-one years, and he never once said he loved me.
Grandpa tapped the table three times before every dinner. Nobody ever asked him why.
I talked to him all night at the hospital. I don't know if he heard a word.
In 2020, scientists recorded the brains of dying hospice patients. Even the ones who couldn't respond still reacted to sound. Hearing may be one of the last things to go.
Phones don't call dead people. Go to bed.
Your best friend Theo believes you instantly. Theo has lived alone with his mom since he was 9.
Okay. Okay. Can you call Elvis?
Day 2. You want proof. So you call the smartest man who ever died.
Hallo? Wer ist da?
lines.caption: Hallo? Wer ist da? (Hello? Who's there?)

lines.text: Real fact: nobody knows Albert Einstein's last words. He said them in German, to a night nurse who didn't speak German.
Mister Einstein, what were your last words?
Ach. Das ist eine lange Geschichte.
lines.caption: Ach. Das ist eine lange Geschichte. (Oh. That's a long story.)

lines.text: He says it in German. You don't speak German either. Click. 28 calls left.
Day 3. You need money. So you call a Wall Street trader who died in 2001.
What should I buy?
Easy. Blockbuster. They just laughed some tiny DVD company out of the room.
True story. In 2000, Netflix offered to sell itself to Blockbuster for 50 million dollars. Blockbuster said no. Ten years later, Blockbuster was bankrupt.
The dead don't know the future. Only their past.
Can you call Elvis?
Theo. No.
Fine. Call my best friend, Sarah. She died in college. Ask her what I did with her red sweater.
Tell her she can keep the sweater. And tell her it was never her fault.
Your mom drops her coffee.
How did you know about the sweater?
That's when you realize what the dead do know. Where they left things.
Real number: American states are holding about 70 billion dollars nobody has claimed. Forgotten bank accounts. Old paychecks. About 1 in 7 Americans has some.
A lot of it belongs to people who died before telling anyone.
There's even a job for this. Heir hunters find the families, and usually keep 10 to 30 percent.
You have 26 calls left. And a phone that can ask the dead directly.
Day 5. Harold. Died in 1998.
Savings account. First Federal. 1983. My daughter never knew.
Harold's daughter gets 42,000 dollars. You keep 20 percent.
And Harold gets his last 10 seconds.
Tell her I'm proud of her.
Day 6. A sailor's pension. Day 9. A safe deposit box in Ohio. Day 14. A piano teacher who buried cash in a coffee can.
Can you call Elvis?
Elvis does not have unclaimed money, Theo.
Every call ends the same way. Money for the family. And 10 seconds for the thing they never said.
Day 26. You have 71,000 dollars. You need 86,000. And you have 4 calls left.
Then the bank calls. The buyer wants to close early. Day 30. Midnight.
And the phone company sends a letter. Grandpa's line gets cut off the same night.
After midnight, no more calls. Ever.
So you stop calling strangers. You call Grandpa's best friend, Eddie. Died in 2009.
Walt? Every year on your grandma's birthday, he bought a savings bond. Never cashed a single one.
That's real too. The U.S. Treasury is holding almost 30 billion dollars in savings bonds nobody ever cashed.
He kept them in a tin. A blue one.
Day 30. The bank lets the family in for one last walk-through.
Second drawer. Behind the tablecloths. A blue tin.
Fifty-one savings bonds. Enough. The house is saved.
But the money was never the point. Under the bonds, there's a note. In Grandpa's handwriting.
Three taps means I love you. I was always too scared to say it out loud. So I said it every night.
Fifty-one years. Three taps a night. He said it more than 18,000 times.
Grandma taps the table three times.
Me too, Walt. Me too.
11:58 p.m. One call left. Two minutes until the line goes dead forever.
You could call anyone. Einstein again. Elvis.
Hey. Can you call...
For once, he doesn't say Elvis.
...my dad?
You hand him the phone.
You don't hear what Theo says. You just watch him talk for 60 seconds. He laughs. Then he cries. Then the line goes dead.
At 3:07 a.m., the disconnected phone rings one last time.
You pick up. There's no voice. Just three soft taps.
Then a click.
Grandma still lives in the house. Theo still asks about Elvis.
Okay, but what if we find another phone?
So, if you had one minute with someone who's gone, who would you call? Tell us in the comments.
